speechtext:
The House resumed from Thursday, January 28, consideration of the motion of Mr. Bouchard:
That a message be sent to the Senate to acquaint Their Honours that this House agrees with amendments 8 and 13(e) made by the Senate to Bill C-84, an Act to amend the Immigration Act, 1976 and the Criminal Code in consequence thereof, but disagrees with amendments 4, 5(a), (b) and (c), 6(a) and (b), 9, 10, 11, 12 and 13(a) because this House believes they contradict the principles of the Bill for the following reasons:
Amendment 4 would exclude only criminals and war criminals from the refugee determination process, but would allow terrorists, spies and subversives to pursue a claim to refugee status, notwithstanding the fact that Article 33 of the UN Convention would permit the removal of these latter individuals to their countries of nationality or permanent residence, even if they were determined to be Convention refugees.
Amendment 5(a) would eliminate the authority of the Minister to direct a ship to leave or not to enter Canadian waters. This amendment would reopen a significant gap in Canada's ability to control its borders.
Amendments 5(b) and (c) arise out of Senate amendment 5(a), which is not acceptable, and are therefore inappropriate.
Amendments 6(a) and (b) would reverse the policy on which the Immigration Act, 1976 was based, which policy was not changed in the Bill as passed by this House. The amendments jeopardize the possibility of successfully prosecuting persons who profit from organizing illegal migration and from counselling fraud among refugee claimants.
Amendments 9 and 10 would restrict the ability of peace officers and immigration officers to act quickly to search for evidence of major offences under the Immigration Act, 1976, in exigent circumstances, where lives are at risk or where evidence with respect to those offences may be lost or destroyed.
Amendments 11 and 12 would restrict the ability of peace officers and immigration officers to execute search warrants which have been duly authorized by a justice of the peace, by denying explicit authority to break open containers where it is reasonably believed evidence will be found and by limiting the authority to execute these warrants at night.
Amendment 13(a) would reduce the initial period of detention without review from seven days to forty-eight hours, which would allow insufficient time for the gathering of information to substantiate allegations or to identify the individual, particularly when large groups of undocumented persons arrive at one time.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before 1 finished speaking yesterday I was beginning to make the points about the two major flaws that we see in the Bill as proposed by the Government.
The first flaw dealt with the decision to incorporate an amendment which would see a boat turned away at the point of entry into Canadian waters. The reason we believe that that particular amendment is seriously flawed is two-fold. First, we may in many cases see legitimate refugees who are turned away without even been given the right to a hearing. We may see a situation similar to what we as a country experienced in the Second World War when shamefully we turned away a boatload of Jewish refugees without giving them any kind of a hearing. As a country, it is not the kind of precedent that we would like to set.
The second flaw is that it permits the shipowner, who is the real mercenary, the rip-off artist, the trader in human flesh, to drop refugees outside the 200 mile boundary thus putting potential refugees at risk of drowning. But that individual will already have cash at hand. He is paid before the people get on the boat. He will drop the refugees outside the 200 mile limit and be gone. He will be laughing all the way to the bank.
If we are going to introduce an amendment, we want to get at these shipowners to discourage them from trading in human flesh. One way would be to accept the Liberal amendment. This would make sure that those refugees who come to Canada are given due process and a fair hearing while the shipowner who trades in human flesh will have his boat and assets seized, will be put in jail and have his boat sold off.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs

speechtext: Good.

speechtext:
Yes, good. That is exactly what we would like to see happen. Unfortunately, in Bill C-84 as it presently exists there is no provision to seize the boat and throw the owner in jail. The boat will be turned away before it actually enters Canadian waters. The Hon. Member will understand that that particular measure will prevent potential legitimate refugees, like the boat people, like the Jewish refugees in the Second World War, from coming to Canada and getting a fair hearing. In the meantime, it will still permit the ship owner to cash in on human flesh. He will be able to take his hundreds of thousands of dollars, drop the refugees outside Canada's territorial waters, and disappear.
The Bill as proposed does not deal with the issue of shipowners who are trading in human flesh. If the Government accepts the Liberal amendment, this would permit the seizure and the sale of the boat, if it is determined it is in Canadian waters illegitimately, and the imprisonment of the ship owner. That is the route we should take.
By turning away a boat, we are violating a UN Convention which provides for due process. We could be turning away legitimate refugees without giving them a fair hearing. Canada is the only nation in the world that has been recognized internationally for its open and generous attitude toward stateless and homeless people. I do not think we want to see that reputation thrown out of the window' by incorporating in law a provision which violates the United Nations Charter.
January 29, 1988

The second part of this Bill which is seriously flawed was not addressed by the Government, either through amendments that had been proposed in the House of Commons by the Liberal Party or amendments that had been proposed in the Senate by all Members of all Parties, including the Independents and the Conservatives. The amendment we would like the Government to accept deals with people who assist and aid refugees.
The Government has introduced legislation which provides that anyone who, without remuneration, out of the goodness of his or her heart, assists a stateless person who may not have proper papers is potentially in violation of the Immigration Act. In many cases, people who flee their homelands for fear of their lives and for the safety of their families may not have proper documentation. The Government wants to implement a measure which would tell any church group, priest, nun or religious person that if he or she tries to help a stateless person who does not have proper papers, he or she could be guilty of a violation of the Immigration Act. We think that is wrong.
Not only do we think that is wrong, Conservative Members in the other place felt so strongly about this issue that they returned a unanimous report condemning the Government for refusing to amend that clause we are discussing today. Not only are the Conservatives in the other place and the Opposition in the House of Commons opposed to these two Draconian measures, many others are as well. For example, Nancy Pocock who works with the Inter-Church Committee for Refugees, has said:
If my Government tells me it is a crime to help these people, I will have to say 1 am obeying a higher law and I am going to continue to help them when they need me.
George Cram of the Inter-Church Committee for Refugees, hardly the subversive trader in human flesh the Government alleges it is trying to curb with this legislation, has said:
I do not want to be guilty of committing an offence for doing humanitarian work. I do not want to feel inside myself that what I am doing is illegal, and I do not want to be liable for prosecution. The offence is what you are creating, not the prosecution.

Mr. Speaker, both the Liberals and the Conservatives in the other place tell us there are two major flaws in the legislation as tabled by the Government. First of all, we have the section prescribing that all ships are to be turned back without allowing the refugees on that ship due process. In that case, Mr. Speaker, ship owners or those who trade in human flesh are not being affected at all. They are not being affected since they already have their money and they can let the refugees disembark at sea.
Mr. Speaker, we suggest the legislation be amended to give the authorities the right to seize the ship and sell it, with the proceeds of such sales going to the Crown, and to jail the ship owner who tries unlawfully to bring people into Canada. This reminds me of the situation in 1979, when we had the so-called "boat people" leaving Vietnam under cover of night. I have
Immigration Act, 1976
several friends who went through this process, and I was part of a group that sponsored them.
At the time, some of these people were unable to leave with the proper documentation, and according to the Bill as it now stands, the fact that I helped people who were without the proper documentation because they were obliged to leave Vietnam under cover of night, would today be a crime. And the same applies to all members of religious groups who try to help people who are stateless or have to leave their country. Although they receive no money, no remuneration for what they do, they will be violating the law by helping refugees.
Mr. Speaker, Canada is the only country in the world that has received international recognition for the role it played in helping people who were leaving Vietnam. We received that recognition because we opened our homes and our hearts to refugees who had no place to stay and who were in fact stateless.
And now we have Bill C-84 and these two measures which, in fact, mean that we do not give due process, we do not give a hearing to people who arrive on ships, even if they happen to be genuine refugees. We are going to turn them back as we turned back the Jews during the Second World War, without giving them a chance to tell their story to our officials and explain how they had to flee their country without the proper documentation.
Second, according to the Bill, Canadian men and women- whether they are priests, nuns, or members of various churches-who try to help people who do not have the proper documentation because they had to flee their country with only the clothes they had on, may be committing a crime by helping refugees who lack proper documentation.
Mr. Speaker, this is so ridiculous that even Conservative senators in the other place objected to the Bill's recommendations out of hand. Both the Liberals in the House of Commons, and the Conservatives in the other place have unanimously rejected the Bill as it now stands.
We already know the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Bouchard) accepted a few amendments because he realized that the Bill as tabled last summer was an overly hasty attempt to react to a situation.

Last summer when the Minister brought in the legislation it was a knee-jerk reaction. He realized that in part, because he did agree to certain amendments which would clarify some of the procedural matters dealing with the Bill. However, he refused to amend the two fundamental clauses of the Bill, and I will tell you why he refused to amend them, Mr. Speaker. I know that this will be provocative, but I hope it will assist Conservative Members in their deliberations on this Bill.
The Government is attempting to use refugees to score political points by whipping up a public frenzy on an issue

Immigration Act, 1976
which is very poorly understood by Canadians. The Government is attempting to use refugees to improve its own standing in the popularity polls. If the Government is not attempting to use refugees in that way, then I challenge it to bring forward two amendments.
First, we should give refugees the right to a full and fair hearing, and that means all refugees, whether alleged or otherwise. If they are proven not to be refugees, they will be deported. That is the law of the land. Second, we should ensure that those people who in the legitimate course of humanitarian good, whether they be members of church groups or are doing it because of a personal commitment, try to help those people who are stateless and homeless, who do not have proper documentation, are not considered criminals. With those two amendments maybe the Government will stop using this issue as a political football and stop exploiting refugees.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, obviously the Hon. Member is very exercised about the Government's strategy on this issue. I would like her to explain to the House why she believes this is part of an electoral strategy by the Government rather than a sincere piece of legislation.

subtopic: IMMIGRATION ACT, 1976 MEASURE TO AMEND-CONSIDERATION OF SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the Government originally introduced this legislation it was supposed to be a response to an "emergency". It was such an emergency that here we are seven months later and the Government did not choose to bring it back for several months. The Government brought in two Bills and this is one. The other Bill was the more reasoned approach.
I believe the reason the Government brought this Bill in last summer, a Bill with very invidious sections dealing with the refusal to grant due process to prospective refugees as well as the refusal to allow Canadians the right, under the auspices of church organizations and private groups, to engage in assisting stateless and homeless peoples, is that it looked at the issue and saw how many people feel. I know people, and I have them in my riding, who see someone coming to Canada without using the normal immigration process and thinking somehow they are getting ahead of everyone else. What they do not realize, and what I alluded to yesterday, is that we have two streams of people coming into this country. One stream is the stateless and homeless; that process is accepted and endorsed by all Canadians. All Canadians believe in it. The other stream is normal immigration.
Because the immigration process is so tight right now, and because there are so many good people who are not allowed to come to Canada because of quotas and other rather severe restrictions, those who are waiting to be reunited with their families feel that somehow if we accept refugees we are lessening their opportunity to have their relatives and friends come into the country. That is not the case, but you have to be
a student of the Immigration Act to even understand the nuances and differences.
Unfortunately, most of us when we read the papers tend to have a knee-jerk reaction to the question of someone arriving here by boat. Persons arriving by boat may indeed be a legitimate refugees who could face death if they went back to their own country. We should not be going after the refugees who may be legitimate and who should have the right to due process. We should be going after the shipowners who are simply attempting to exploit people by accepting money for passage. They will be off on the high seas and the people we will be going after are those who may need our help and a home in Canada.
1 think the Government is trying to cover up its own incompetence in dealing with the question of immigration by isolating certain instances and trying to get the public whipped into a frenzy on an issue which is very poorly understood. The Government has a responsibility to clear up the two-track system, one being refugees and the other normal immigration, and deal with the real culprits, the traders in human flesh, not simply those who may be legitimately seeking a new home.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had the opportunity to represent Canada at an executive counsel meeting of the UN High Commissioner for Refugees the first week of October, 1987. I had the opportunity there to discuss this issue with representatives of most of the nations in the world who are involved in providing significant support for refugees. Perhaps even more importantly, I also had the opportunity to meet with the legal affairs division of the UNHCR. As a consequence of that in depth discussion about Canadian law and the law of other countries, I have been able to go on public platforms in Canada and assert that the legal protection for refugee claimants under Canada's new legislation, a combination of Bill C-84 and Bill C-55, will be a standard to which the rest of the world can aspire. I have said rather flatly that there is no legal system in the world which will come close to matching Canada's new system in providing legal protection for refugee claimants.
I simply want to ask the Hon. Member this. If she believes in what she has been saying to this House today, will she have the courage to stand in her place and name a single country in this whole world that will provide better legal protection to refugee claimants than the projected Canadian system-one country, I challenge her?

Bill. It is a blight on a very laudable Canadian record around the world in accepting and welcoming bona fide refugees to this country.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member has just admitted the difficulties with this legislation. He said that the people who are on that boat will not be given individual due process. He just said it is up to the Minister. If the Minister is under political pressure and feels like turning the boat back, it is going to go back. These people, who could be bona fide refugees and who should have their cases heard individually, are going to be denied that due process. They will not be given the kind of protection which has been afforded to every refugee claimant in Canada and that will be afforded under certain clauses of Bill C-55, which is not the Bill we are discussing today.
Bill C-84 was a knee-jerk reaction by the Government at a time when a boat was coming towards Canada. Frankly, I do not want to leave due process and the protection of prospective refugees in the hands of a Minister who may be responding to political pressure in the way he did last summer when he introduced this piece of garbage we are now considering.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am happy to join in this debate on the proposed Senate amendments to Bill C-84. I am not pleased, however, because of the Bill itself, which 1 join with members of my caucus and many other Members of the House in opposing as an attack on Canadian humanitarianism and a reaction to some of the darkest tendencies in the Canadian nation-a desire to close the doors on refugees. That is a very partisan and political move of the worst sort.
I want to speak with satisfaction on amendments which would make it possible to improve this Bill somewhat. If the Government is determined to go through with it, let us have at least the removal of some of the elements of the Bill which would interfere with the desire of so many Canadians to provide refuge to persons who are in danger of life and limb in the countries from which they have fled.
Immigration Act, 1976
I want to recognize the observations of the critic on immigration in our caucus, my good friend the Member for Spadina (Mr. Heap), who spoke very well earlier this week in support of the proposed amendments. He indicated what the strategy of the Government has been. It is worth spotlighting some of what has happened on this matter earlier before considering the particular amendment which is before us this morning, that being Amendment 4 from the Senate.
As my friend indicated, it took a little while for the policy of the Government to become clear. In the first months of this Parliament the Commons Committee on Labour, Employment and Immigration was at work considering the question of how to treat refugees and considering an important document, a report commissioned by the previous Government which Rabbi Gunther Plaut produced. This report was in the best tradition of Canadian humanitarianism. The committee of Members from the government caucus and the two opposition caucuses, in lesser numbers, worked together on consideration of that report making representations to the House, and, consequently, to the Government and Canadian people, on how refugees should be treated.
It became clear later that at the same time a task force on saving money in the Government and on the efficiency of government operations was at work. That task force was under the direction of the then Deputy Prime Minister, Erik Nielsen. It became clear when that report was released later that a very different agenda was being pursued at the highest levels of the immigration department and within the Government itself. That agenda looked to the saving of money. It was suggested that some $60 million could be saved and it became clear that a good deal of that could be saved in the area of immigration by tightening up in particular ways.
As my friend the Member for Spadina indicated, the Government never responded to the report of the Standing Committee on Labour, Employment and Immigration. That report recognized the contributions and recommendations of Rabbi Gunther Plaut and called on the Canadian Government to improve and streamline the system for refugee determination. It called upon the Government to provide resources so there would be enough people to carry through the process of determination, get rid of the backlog, and ensure that Canadian humanitarianism was manifested in procedure as well as in principle, so that persons would have their status recognized at an early stage and could consequently settle down to life among the Canadian people. The Government, which was preoccupied with its agenda of the Nielsen task force, never commented on or reacted that report of the committee.
In the summer of 1986 refugees arrived and the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) himself spoke in a commendable way on the traditions of Canadian humanitarianism. In the summer of 1987 more refugees arrived by boat on the Atlantic coast. We observed the most remarkable night-against- day turn by the Prime Minister as he began to pander to very different tendencies, those of the minority that is prepared to close the door, the minority which fears refugees, particularly

January 29, 1988
Immigration Act, 1976
from the southern hemisphere, the minority which wants still to have a white Canada as some Canadians have always wanted. Playing to those tendencies, to prejudice in Canada, some of the best hopes that had been manifested by Ministers of the Government earlier were suddenly contradicted.
Late in the year I spotlighted a statement made by the Minister for Employment and Immigration who, speaking in the spring, promised a campaign against racism. He recognized that the way to deal with racism, prejudice, and discrimination in Canada was to deal with the ignorance on which they feed. During the summer the Government pandered to ignorance and stupidity and the Minister for Employment and Immigration (Mr. Bouchard) has not launched such a campaign. The Government has been strangely silent in developing race relations policy in the area of multiculturalism.
That failure is directly related to this most unfortunate decision to play to Canadian prejudice generally, to bring in legislation, and to allow individual case situations to be made known to the Canadian public. These leaks are still going on. There has been controversy in the House, appropriate or otherwise, in the last weeks on certain cases. How could that controversy occur if it were not that individual files were being made known to the media? It is clear that information is leaking out from the immigration department. That is surely being done quite deliberately to continue pandering to Canadian prejudice.
Not only do we have silence as far as a campaign against racism is concerned, but the Government is allowing officials to pander to those feelings by putting out partial information and allowing the press to build up the kind of anger that can develop among people when they think that something terribly wrong has been allowed to happen.
This kind of attack on Canadian humanitarianism is not just an attack on the expression at the national level, where the Inter-Church Committee, for example, has been eloquently leading, supported by lawyers who have been working in the immigration area for years who know the shortcomings of the system, who want improvement of it, and who certainly never expected that the Government would bring in the kind of vicious legislation which we have before us. It is not an attack on a national activity or on people active in particular in the City of Toronto where so many persons wanting to put refugee claims forward first appear.
In the City of Thunder Bay in northwestern Ontario, many miles from Toronto, only a few score of persons are accepted each year as government-sponsored refugees. In my community the expression of Canadian humanitarianism through the Friends of Refugees organization and through members of the Thunder Bay Multiculturalism Association has been one of the most heartening expressions of Canadian humanitarianism. This movement was fostered and developed in the mid and late 1970s by the Government itself. When people from Vietnam were coming to Canada great encouragement was given to individual Canadians, groups, and churches in particular, to
undertake the work of providing refuge to people, supporting them in Canada, and assisting them to become established. That work has been brilliantly successful.
In my own church in Thunder Bay, St. Paul's United Church, I have been contributing for a year or more in support of a refugee project. I mention that without wanting to arouse envy anywhere else because I could name other churches in the City of Thunder Bay that are very active.
I hesitate to single out names, but I think of the efforts of Lloyd Jones in Thunder Bay and on the national level and of Mel McLaughlin and others in the Friends of Refugees organization. These are manifestations of the best desire of Canadians to allow our rich country to provide the refuge that people from other parts of the world need.
What have we seen in contradiction to this from the Government? We see a particularly refusal to recognize the legitimate problems that exist in immigration. Our caucus realizes that illigitimate refugee claims are made occasionally and procedures are necessary to deal with those. However, there is not the kind of clandestine entry in those cases on which the Government wants to focus. There is not the lack of documents, very often in those cases. Usually someone outside Canada is involved in aiding in the offence of sending bogus refugees to Canada who very often arrive with legitimate documentation. These people who arrive from Portugal, Brazil or perhaps Turkey would not be caught by the Government's legislation.
Those people who arrive from Central and South America, where they have been made refugees by the civil wars that rage in a number of those countries, are the owner who arrive without documentation, because they would not be able to obtain the visas or other papers to make them legitimate entrants to Canada. These people are very often regarded in their own countries as subversives and may well be shot by the death squads in a number of those countries. These are the people who will be caught, and those who assist them in coming to Canada, recognizing that the United States is much less sensitive to the legitimate refugee claims of these persons, could very easily be caught by this legislation and end up with their vehicles confiscated, facing fines and conceivably prison terms.
The Government, which has broken its word on so many other matters, gives us asssurances in the House that it would not act or authorize prosecutions against such persons. That is simply not acceptable. The Government does not have the credibility with this Parliament and the people of Canada to be trusted with such promises.
Therefore, speaking on behalf of constituents, friends and persons whom I admire very much in Thunder Bay, I oppose what the Government has put forward and support the amendments put before us from the Senate, and specifically
January 29, 1988

the amendment put forward by the Member for York West (Mr. Marchi) dealing with amendment No. 4.
Let me note the significance of the amendments put forward by the Member for York West in regard to Central America. When the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) visited Central America recently, he made a number of observations on the situation. Probably the most remarkable and controversial was his suggestion that those involved in the contra effort against the Sandinistas in Nicaragua might be allowed entry into Canada, to allow refuge to these freedom fighters of President Reagan.
Of course, one must explain this somewhat. These people are counter-revolutionaries, the henchmen of the Somoza regime in Nicaragua. They are the people who exploited the Nicaraguan people until the people were successful in the Sandinista revolution in overthrowing that dictatorship, supported so long by the United States. They achieved a government which, if not for the war, would have made the kinds of advances for Nicaraguan people that the Cuban revolution has made over 30 years on that island. However, the American government has chosen to support these henchmen of the Somoza regime.
The President who should be an example of truth to the so-called free world has allowed his integrity to be completely destroyed by attempting to turn these counter-revolutionaries in Nicaragua, who worked for that previous dictatorship, into freedom fighters. That has been one of the abominations of the 1980's, and has only been intensified every time the President speaks about strengthening democracy in the 1980's, as he did in the State of the Union Address. That is an abomination when American money is destroying property, slaying Nicaraguans and being used to destroy the efforts of aid workers from other countries to support the Nicaraguan people in rebuilding their revolution.
In El Salvador death squad members in the El Salvadorean military, in this case supporting a government that is fighting a revolution, had launched an attack on a restaurant, killing several Americans, among others. According to a recent report, it had been determined at a trial that these death squad members had been involved in a political act. When we see the murder of off-duty Americans, of civilians and persons in a social setting by members of the El Salvadorean forces being regarded as a political act, surely it is not possible to argue against the reality of circumstances that create refugees who have every right to the safety that Canada can provide.
The Hon. Member for York West, in his amendment specifically dealing with amendment No. 4, is focusing on a matter of enormous importance, an amendment which would not preclude from the refugee determination process persons who might be security risks. That focuses on a particular item in which the legislation the Government has put forward is in fact a contradiction to the United Nations convention on refugees.
In this respect the Parliamentary Secretary was posing questions to the Member for Hamilton East (Ms Copps) in
Immigration Act, 1976
which he wanted to find some country that was better than Canada in providing refuge. 1 am not an expert on this internationally and would not be able to name a country which is better, although I think it would be a terrible judgment on the western world in our time if there is no country that has better law than Canada. It would be a terrible judgment on the whole western world if western humanity has sunk to the level of violation of U.N. convention which the Government proposes to put forward.
The U.N. convention allows persons, even those who may be security risks, to put forward a claim for refugee status. subtopic: SUPREME COURT
SUPREME COURT
subsubtopic: JUDGMENT ON ABORTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday the Supreme Court rendered a judgment on abortion. I should like to single out three individuals who opened this debate 20 years ago: Dr. Lise Fortier of Montreal, Marion Powell of Toronto, and Dr. Peter Gillett of Montreal.

The Supreme Court of Canada rendered a historical judgment yesterday. It struck down a law that treated women unequally. The judges found this law unconstitutional because women in some provinces were found to have more choice available to them concerning their reproduction than women in other provinces. Under the Charter of Rights and Freedoms every individual must be treated equally. Therefore, this law must be changed so that all Canadian women have access to the same services and options across the country.
I call on the Government to introduce legislation in the House that will recognize that women must be treated equally across Canada. I also call on the Government to recognize that the Supreme Court of Canada has given the federal Parliament the role of regulating how, when, and where these services will be made available and how we will balance the competing interests in this issue.
Now that we have been given this trust, let us proceed cautiously and wisely. Let us recognize that all women must be treated equally and have the same options and services.

PENSIONS-CALL FOR WITHDRAWAL OF BILL C-33
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Wednesday the Government decided at the last minute not to proceed with debate on Bill C-33, the Bill which would have deindexed future pensions for 250,000 federal government employees.

My colleagues and I plan to oppose the Bill with every tool at our disposal. A delay of the Bill is not good enough, however. The current situation creates uncertainty for federal employees which should be ended now.
I call on the Government to announce that it is abandoning its proposal to deindex federal employees' pensions and to consult with the Public Service unions so that the other parts of the Bill which would give civil servants direct input into the management of their pensions can be implemented quickly.
I urge my Conservative colleagues from the national capital region to stand up and to join the New Democrats to say publicly that Bill C-33 is a bad Bill and that the proposal to deindex federal employees' pensions should be scrapped.

subtopic: SUPREME COURT DECISION HAILED AS VICTORY
SUPREME COURT DECISION HAILED AS VICTORY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is the view of the New Democratic Party that the exact opposite should be the case to what the Hon. Member for York South-Weston (Mr. Nunziata) has just proclaimed.
In its historic decision yesterday, the Supreme Court of Canada made absolutely clear that the country's abortion law, Section 251 of the Criminal Code, is a violation of the life, liberty and security of the person guaranteed in Section 7 of the Charter.
The words of the Chief Justice could not be clearer. He stated:
Section 251 clearly interferes with a woman's physical and bodily integrity. Forcing a woman, by threat of criminal sanction, to carry a fetus to term unless she meets certain criteria unrelated to her own priorities and aspirations, is a profound interference with a woman's body and thus an infringement of security of the person.
In the words of Madam Justice Bertha Wilson:
Section 251 of the Criminal Code, which limits the pregnant woman's access to abortion, violates her right to life, liberty and security of the person within the meaning of Section 7 of the Charter-
The decision is clear. Let the Government not attempt to fudge it or circumvent it in any way, or try to limit this great victory achieved by the women of Canada.

subtopic: NATO-POSITION OF NEW DEMOCRATIC PARTY
NATO-POSITION OF NEW DEMOCRATIC PARTY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this weekend, in what promises to be a real Donnybrook, the New Democratic Party will review its defence policy, especially with respect to Canada's participation in NATO. Many Canadians will recall that the NDP released a defence policy paper this past summer reaffirming its policy of withdrawal from NATO. However, the unpopularity of this policy, as noted in the polls which the NDP so avidly read, has called for a review of the policy.
Canada now waits with bated breath for an answer. Will pragmatism win out over principle? Will New Democrats seek salvation through polls? Are we seeing the emergence of a new New Democratic Party? Or is it something more sinister?
Perhaps the NDP defence policy is all that stands between the long awaited NDP-Liberal coalition. Will members of the NDP in their unseemly haste to jump into bed with an already amorous Liberal Party shed their principles at the door? Will the fruits of this union be an Old Democratic Party or a New Liberal Party?
Stay tuned next week for the dramatic conclusion of this political Peyton Place.

subtopic: IMMIGRATION ACT, 1976 MEASURE TO AMEND-CONSIDERATION OF SENATE AMENDMENTS

speechtext: The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Bouchard in relation to the amendments made by the Senate to Bill C-84, an Act to amend the Immigration Act, 1976 and the Criminal Code in consequence thereof, and on the amendment of Mr. Marchi (p. 12340).

subtopic: IMMIGRATION ACT, 1976 MEASURE TO AMEND-CONSIDERATION OF SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise to speak on this Bill, but I am somewhat saddened that it is back here for ongoing debate. I would have hoped, along with our colleagues around this room who have an open heart and open mind, and along with the other place, which carefully studied this Bill that was sent to them under emergency circumstances last August, that we would have settled the whole issue and would now be in a position to move forward with respect to refugees who are leaving the lands of their birth and seeking asylum in other countries, certainly not always from their own choice. To become a refugee and to have to leave one's home country is no easy decision. They certainly are coming from places of turmoil.
I would like to point out that we were called back during a summer recess to deal with this Bill as an emergency situation because some boats landed off the coast of Nova Scotia. I would suggest that some people were very traumatized at what looked like an invasion by some one hundred and seventy some souls.
We had been calling on the Government of Canada for nearly three years to bring in comprehensive refugee legislation which would be seen as fair, expeditious and which would assist in the curbing of abuse to the system. There was no question that there was a need to curb the abuse which was taking place.
The Government had the good fortune to receive the wise counsel of Rabbi Plaut, who tabled the Plaut report. It had the wise counsel of a standing committee of this House which studied at great length complicated and heart-wrenching
Immigration Act, 1976
concerns and considerations which face refugees. When it brought this regressive and repressive Bill into the House it heard some very enlightened observations and some very concrete suggestions of ways to improve the thrust of this Bill to ensure that it would not be in contravention of international law and that it would not be in contravention of our Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
We also heard from the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees, and I will come back to that in a moment. We thought the Government would have welcomed all this wise counsel and would have adjusted the Bill, accepting the amendments which were put forth under great duress because there was not the kind of consultation we would have liked. In light of the fact the Government saw this as an acute emergency, the amendments were brought forward. Yet the Government did not accept those amendments. It pushed the Bill through the House with its massive majority. Fortunately, collectively in that other place, the Senators found reason to correct this Bill. They found reasons to make very strong recommendations for change. They unanimously agreed to send 18 recommendations back to this House, 18 amendments on a Bill that has been hanging around under a supposed emergency state since last August. The Minister saw fit to accept only four of those amendments which, in a sense, were for clarification or with respect to language. However, he rejected the others, the major ones. I gather that there were four language amendments and three other small corrections which were made to the Bill. When it came to the major recommendations we did not see any forward movement on the part of the Government irrespective of the careful and thoughtful consideration that had been given to the legislation in the other place.
The areas of the Bill which deal with its heart and soul, that were refused consideration by the Government, were those which addressed the powers of authority to detain identified refugee claimants for long periods without review. The second area was the right to turn ships back at sea if suspected of carrying illegal aliens. The third was with respect to the right to prosecute anyone, including church groups, who might be found to have helped claimants who did not seemingly have valid visas or valid passports.
Let us consider in what areas the Government chose not to accept the major recommendations. The first area which strikes me as being horrendous is the following. If we cast our minds back to ships being turned back at sea we could consider the Vietnamese boat people and the sight of people floating unprotected on waters. I cannot believe that the Minister did not take the counsel that was given to him on four occasions. He chose to ignore that counsel.
I have in my hand a letter sent by Mr. Jean-Pierre Hocke, the United Nation's High Commissioner for Refugees. The letter is from Geneva and dated August 12, 1987. The letter is addressed to the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. COMMONS DEBATES
January 29, 1988
Immigration Act, 1976
Clark) and the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Bouchard). It states:
I have the honour to refer to an amendment to the Immigration Act 1976 (Bill C-84) which the Government of Canada has most recently tabled in Parliament. My Office fully understand the Canadian Government's preoccupation regarding abuses of procedures for the determination of refugees status and related problems. Certain provisions of the proposed legislation, however, give rise to serious concern in as much as lack of procedural safeguards could risk exposing bona fide asylum seekers and refugees to forcible return to territories where their lives or freedom would be threatened (refoulement).
That has been described and explained as refoulement.
This pertains in particular to Clause No. 8 of the Bill introducing a new Section 91.1 in the Act relating to the authority to direct ships to leave or not to enter the internal waters of Canada or the territorial sea of Canada, apparently without examination of passengers' status. The principle of non-refloulement to which Canada fully adheres as a party to the 1951 UN Convention Relating to the Status of Refugees and the 1967 Protocol there to enjoins any action on the part of states which may result in refoulement.
The same principle requires the adoption of appropriate procedures to ensure observance with guarantees, no less effective than those available, to persons claiming refugee status in Canada. The adoption of such procedures would be consistent with the contents of Clause 1 Sections 2.1 (A) and (D) of the Bill which state-"to preserve for persons in genuine need of protection access to the procedures for determining refugee claims" and "-the fulfilment of Canada's obligations in respect of internationally protected persons".
The letter goes on to state:
As you are no doubt aware the situations now being faced are not unique to Canada. Institution of the procedural safeguards referred to above would serve as an important example to the international community and help preserve the principle of asylum throughout the world.
In light of these considerations I am confident that all persons who seek Canada's protection will be afforded adequate procedural safeguards against refoulement and that these will be incorporated in the operative part of the Bill in question.
While these are my Office's initial reactions to the proposed legislation, my Representative in Ottawa may convey further comments on these and related important issues.
Please accept the assurances of my highest consideration. Jean-Pierre Hocke, United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees.
I find it quite astonishing that with the remarks and the concerns brought to the attention of all by the High Commissioner and by Rabbi Plaut, reinforced by representations and presentations, that the Minister still stubbornly refuses to change that clause in Bill C-84. It would seem that the Government has truly not reflected. If it has reflected, and it has come to some very poor conclusions. It is beyond me how the Minister could not understand and accept that particular amendment. It is abhorrent to think that this would not be considered vital. To turn a boat back without knowing whether or not there are true refugees on board is inappropriate action. It is not what exists in the hearts and souls of most Members of the House of Commons.
How do we know who is on board? How do we know if they are really in need or not? How do we know from where they are really coming? How do we know their ages? How do we know the state of their health? How do we know the state of the boat? The unknown is a big variable in the consideration of
this matter, something which the Government has simply not addressed in this Bill.
I suggest that a more intelligent approach would be to have sent out messages that we have no patience for people who deal in human flesh. We have no patience for people who will not respect the lives and the rights of individuals. We have no respect for smugglers and for people who are taking advantage of those in need. Those are the types of messages we want to get across. That is what Canadians would have said while saying, "We are open to accepting and understanding the plight of the refugee".
I would now like to deal with the question of fairness. Perhaps the Government does not think that fairness and equal treatment across the land is something that Canadians want. I think the Government has misjudged in that respect. People arriving on boats as legitimate refugees will be turned around in Canadian waters or outside our waters. I do not know how we will force these boats to turn around. I guess we will pull out our big guns, or perhaps our nuclear submarines will force them to turn around and go the other way. This will force, without much knowledge, the return of people to lord knows where. It will put them in jeopardy and danger.
However, if people in similar circumstances are lucky enough to board a plane and land at one of our airports then they will be given refugee status. They will be given some form of decent treatment. At least someone will look at their papers and do some checking. If they come by boat, they receive different treatment. I do not think that that is correct. That is not the type of system we want. We do not want a two-class, two-category system. In Canada there is one category and one class. The laws are the same for everyone, and everyone should be treated equally.
How do we discourage smugglers, ship captains, and owners of the boats? The manner in which to do that is to pull the boats into safe harbour, check and verify the condition of the passengers and find out if they are refugees, but at the same time take the captain of that boat, fine him, put him in jail, put him on trial, and confiscate the right to that boat. I guarantee in no short order the message will get out across the land and across the sea, "Don't go to Canada that way. You will be escorted directly to jail. Do not pass go. You are not going to collect 200 bucks", for those of you who know the old Monopoly rules. "The rules of the game in Canada are that you cannot bring people into this land by boat and be expected to be treated as a hero, or go free and turn around in order that your next friend can try to do the same thing and dump human cargo so that they are floating out in the sea, or they walk into a strange place, or they run away in fear".
That is not the way people are integrated into this society. Canada has been built with refugees. Often as I drive down the road in my particular riding I think of the Vietnamese boat people, and how proud I was to be among those citizens who
January 29, 1988

sponsored a family and helped bring them to this country and saw to their establishment. I now know many of those children and see how marvelously they have adapted to this land, and how beautifully they have enriched our landscape by the tapestry that they have helped to weave to strengthen this country. They have been entrepreneurs and have brought economic prosperity to this country. More than 100,000 Vietnamese boat people came to this land. Other refugee movements have been given safe harbour in this country, for example, Polish, Hungarian, Czechoslovakian, and Sri Lanka.
Now we have two types of laws for how someone gets to this country, and two types of circumstances under which someone is considered as a refugee. That is thoroughly unacceptable. 1 find it unbelievable that the Minister was not prepared to change that aspect of the Bill.
The second aspect of the Bill that 1 find mind-boggling is that any group that enables, helps, guides, or counsels refugees, particularly those who might be here without valid visas or passports, will be prosecuted. I do not know where the Minister thinks these people who run away from persecution and possible death might go to pick up this valid paper. Do they say, "Just a minute, don't shoot me. I have to go and talk to the embassy and see if they will give me a piece of paper so I can be validated. Wait until I go and check my health. Wait until I have some tests". What type of crazy world does the Minister think we are living in? This is absolute hypocrisy.
We are either a country of receipt that is open to refugees who seek safe haven on our shores, or we are not. Certainly many of those refugees will not have valid papers at the time that they arrive. That does not mean that we do not want to get validation, or do proper checking. Certainly we do. There is a procedure and a manner in which to do that without misusing the force of the Government and misrepresenting the will of the Canadian people.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to make a few comments on Bill C-84. 1 listened to the Parliamentary Secretary attack the Opposition for what he called a filibuster. 1 do not accept that. We are dealing with legislation that is fundamentally flawed, legislation which the churches, the Canadian Bar Association and every single witness who appeared before the Senate committee, except government witnesses, indicated was fundamentally flawed and needed many changes. The Parliamentary Secretary has said that the Opposition is responsible for a filibuster, but we are doing our duty by trying to expose the flaws in this Bill. I think that is fundamentally wrong on his part.
I appreciate having this chance to make one last appeal to the Government to adopt a reasoned and humane policy toward refugees in Canada rather than to turn its back on those people. What we need now from the Government is leadership. Instead, it is creating fear and panic and then pandering to the very fear and panic the Government itself has created. We want a policy that is in accordance with our own Charter Rights and a policy that is in accordance with our international commitments.
A little over a year ago, we received from the United Nations High Commission for Refugees the Nansen award. That award did not go to the Canadian Government, it went to the Canadian people because of their attitude toward refugees. We have a good record and that good record was evidenced last summer when a boatload of refugee claimants landed in Nova Scotia. A woman met them with tea and cookies, a tradition of Canadian hospitality. That is the tradition of the Canadian people, but the Government seems intent upon destroying that good record and so this legislation, Bill C-84, as well as Bill C-55, are before us. Those Bills are undercutting our ability to receive refugees and are certainly undercutting our international standing.
1 would like to say a few things about the importance of ensuring that Canadian laws conform with the Charter. Yesterday, we received the historic decision from the Supreme Court on the Henry Morgentaler case. That decision indicated that the Charter had to be obeyed and respected. The Charter is the fundamental law of Canada. It is not just a high-sounding statement of principle or desired goals, but is the fundamental law, and other laws must be brought into accordance with it.
The Senate report on Bill C-84 quoted the Ontario Court of Appeal's ruling in Reference re Education Act of Ontario and Minority Language Education Rights of 1984. The Ontario Court of Appeal said then:
Immigration Act, 1976
The judiciary is not the sole guardian of the constitutional rights of Canadians. Parliament and the provincial Legislatures are equally responsible to ensure that the rights conferred by the Charter are upheld.
If the Government will not do that, and obviously it is not with Bill C-84, then it is the responsibility of the Opposition and that is what opposition Members are trying to do by speaking on this Bill.
Mr. Justice Dickson, as he then was, writing for the Supreme Court of Canada in Hunter v. Southam of 1984, said much the same thing. He said:
It is the Legislature's responsibility to enact legislation that embodies appropriate safeguards to comply with the Constitution's requirements. It should not fall to the courts to fill in the details that will render legislative lacunae constitutional.
We cannot look to the courts to do our work. If so, we abdicate the trust the people of Canada gave us in the last election, a trust this Government has betrayed in so many different ways.
Passing legislation like Bill C-84, legislation that runs counter to the Charter, is a mammoth hoax on the Canadian people, and an expensive hoax. This legislation will be struck down in certain important provisions. Then it will have to go back to the drawing board.
The Government has received clear indications from organizations such as the Canadian Bar Association that the legislation is flawed. Why does it not attempt to clean up the legislation rather than pretend that it will somehow meet the situation while it knows very well that it will not?
It is interesting that the Government has promised to establish an international institute on human rights. The InterChurch Committee for Refugees had some interesting comments on Bill C-84. It said:
Canada can only remain credible in the international human rights theatres if human rights are fully respected in Canada. The department cannot afford to remain aloof from policies and practices in Canada which threaten or undermine human rights.
It is a matter of deep concern for this department-
The committee is referring here to the Department of External Affairs.
-to launch a centre which focuses on Canada's interest in human rights overseas into the same Parliamentary Session which could pass refugee related Bill C-84 at home. This Bill is a flagrant attack on fundamental rights and freedoms in Canada. By relying on a questionable definition of emergency to justify its clearly excessive measures, it will lower the threshold for Charter Section 1 arguments. If Section 1 can be widely applied for such questionable reasons, the power of every other section of our Charter is reduced. Worse, other states will assume that if Canada does this, it can be considered acceptable.
Instead of having legislation that is in accordance with the Canadian tradition of openness toward refugees, instead of having legislation that is in accordance with our own Charter of Rights and Freedoms, instead of having legislation that is in accordance with the spirit of international covenants which Canada has signed, we have Bill C-84.

January 29, 1988
Immigration Act, 1976
The Government attempted, both last summer when it first introduced this legislation and just this past week, to create a climate of panic and fear so that this legislation would be stampeded through the House of Commons. For example, just two weeks ago, we heard of the case of Mahmoud Mohammad, a convicted terrorist who came to Canada as an immigrant. This case suddenly surfaced in the press. The Government used it as an attempt to justify quick passage of Bill C-84.
There are two questions I would like to raise about this case. Why was the story about Mahmoud Mohammad leaked just as the Government was preparing to reintroduce Bill C-84? I do not know the answer to that question, but there is at least the possibility of a manipulated leak designed to create the climate of fear. We have seen the Government do that before and certainly it arouses that kind of suspicion in my mind.
Second, what does the Mahmoud Mohammad case have to do with Bill C-84? The answer is that it has absolutely nothing to do with Bill C-84 except in the mind of the Government which is trying to link that case with the passage of this Bill. Mohammad did not come here as a refugee. If Bill C-84 and Bill C-55 had been in place, he still would have come here. He arrived in Canada and was accepted as an immigrant because the Government did not properly apply its own regulations, regulations which were already in place. A convicted terrorist arrived in Canada after warnings had been issued because CSIS was having a shift change. To try to use this failure as a reason for putting in place the Draconian measures of Bill C-84 is unconscionable.
My colleague, the Hon. Member for Spadina (Mr. Heap), quoted from a Winnipeg Free Press editorial of January 22 which said:
These are the ministers who claim that Canada needs tough new immigration laws which could be used to send genuine political refugees back to face potential imprisonment, torture or death. Their action demonstrates that, far from draconian new laws, what this country needs most is the competent and honest enforcement of the ones we have.
Competent and honest enforcement of the present legislation, and perhaps some competency on the government side would help as well.
We all recognize that there is a need for tightening the refugee determination process. This has been recognized for a long time. It was recognized by the previous Government which did not take any action on it, but it did appoint the Plaut commission. When that report was brought in, in the early days of the present Government, it did not take any action. Instead, it referred the whole issue to the Standing Committee on Employment and Immigration. When that committee brought in its report the Government did not take any action. It did not even respond to the report, although both the Plaut commission and the standing committee made some very reasonable suggestions that would have helped deal with the question of the backlog of refugees.
The churches made recommendations and the Government did not choose to act. As a result, the situation began to snowball. Canada began to get a reputation as a country where people could make bogus refugee claims and get away with it, certainly for a fair period of time. The Government chose not to act. Perhaps it felt it did not need to. As a result, we had a gradual buildup in the backlog until over 20,000 people are waiting for some kind of final determination of their status.
The Plaut report, the standing committee report, and the churches all recommended a process that would have been speedier, fair, with a reasonable appeal process, and would not have dragged on allowing people making bogus refugee claims to stay in Canada for four and five years. Instead, the whole process would have been through in a matter of some four months. If people were going to be staying here for only four months, it would not be worth their while to pay the very large fees to these unscrupulous refugee or immigration counsellors. However, the Government chose not to act on those recommendations.
Instead, last spring, Bill C-55 was introduced. It was not brought to the House for debate until June. Then there was just a few hours of debate and the House recessed for the summer. Then there was this panic notice that went out in the summer when 174 Sikhs landed in Nova Scotia. The House was called back for a so-called emergency, which I presume still exists, to deal with this issue. Both Bill C-55 and Bill C-84 were brought before us. There was no great emergency. There was a crisis which had gradually been building and which needs government action, but it did not develop suddenly last summer as the Government tried to pretend.
The panic reaction which the Government tried to create and manipulate is not, I submit, the proper climate for dealing with issues fundamentally affecting human rights. They affect human rights in Canada and Canada's standing in the world. They affect the fundamental position individual Canadians are taking towards some of the most disadvantaged people in our world. So much of the focus of the Government has been upon those who are unscrupulous and who do not deserve refugee status. We agree that action has to be taken against those people, but in doing so the Government is going to hurt some of the most disadvantaged people in our world. We are talking about refugees. We talk of them as something we want to push off to one side instead of saying, "Here are fellow human beings who need our assistance and who are speaking to the very depths of our humanity". Instead of responding in a full and free way, the Government is taking Draconian measures which are going to make it more difficult for Canadians to live up to the kind of reputation we achieved over the past 40 years when we received some 400,000 refugees into Canada. We know those refugees made a great contribution to Canadian life. Yet now we are closing the doors.
I want to look just briefly at the provision in this legislation for turning back boats. The Senate wanted to amend that provision, but the Government chose to keep it as it is. We have all heard many times about the disgraceful situation
January 29, 1988

which took place in 1939 when a ship left Germany with 907 Jews and attempted to sail to different countries, including Canada, only to be turned away. That is the Canadian contribution to the Holocaust. We sent those people back to Germany where they faced extermination. That is a black mark upon Canadian history.
Since then we have not had a great many people who have attempted to come to Canada by boat as unsolicited refugees. In 1986 we had a boatload of Tamils who landed off the East Coast of Canada. In 1987 we had 174 Sikhs. That is hardly a major problem. We have a backlog of some 20,000 people in the system, yet the Government brings in this legislation dealing with boat people as though somehow it will solve the problem.
The fact is that the whole idea of people coming here by boat has some symbolism, so that people had the sense we were going to be invaded by an armada. I remember one of the Parliamentary Secretaries, the Hon. Member for Surrey- White Rock-North Delta (Mr. Friesen), talking about five billion people in our world, all of them perhaps coming to Canada. We had that kind of foolish attempt to create panic in the Canadian people. In comparison to the 20,000 backlog, the coming to Canada of boat people is not a major problem.
The Government's ability, under this Bill, to turn a boat back and refuse it entry into Canadian ports is not going to be any real deterrent to any of the people who are organizing these bogus refugee schemes. If the boat that landed in Canada had been seized and the captain arrested or imprisoned, and a stiff fine had been imposed, perhaps that might have been a little bit more of a deterrent. At the same time, by turning boats around and not allowing them to land in Canada, you reduce the possibility of genuine refugees being heard. We regret that, yet the Government has not seen fit to change it. In the past Canada has been concerned about other countries, such as some in Southeast Asia, for example, taking the same position which the Conservative Government is now taking.
In conclusion, this Bill undermines the principles of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms. It undermines the spirit of Canadian commitment to international covenants. It destroys the ability of Canadians to live up to the spirit of openness and generosity to disadvantaged people who come to Canada as refugees. It does not give the protection against bogus refugees which is required, and works against genuine refugees. I urge the Government to look again at this Bill and to bring in the policy which it says it wants to have, that is, a fair refugee determination policy which is humane and open.

in goals with regard to this legislation and the companion legislation.
The Member brought up the issue of boats. 1 do not know whether he has had the opportunity to see refugees in various situations in West Germany, Denmark, or Elolland. People there who make refugee claims do not have the same freedom of movement that we have in this country, but they are safe and healthy. They have food, they have shelter, and they have protection.
The Opposition is urging this Elouse to send a signal to the people in those camps that they should take the risk of putting themselves in the hands of unscrupulous ship captains. These are not captains of passenger boats such as Members of this Chamber take on cruises. They go in the hold of a ship which may or may not be seaworthy and are under the care and control of a crew which may or may not be skilled, with or without doctors, with or without adequate food, and with or without adequate sanitation.
They would tell them to leave the safety that they have in Germany, Britain, or Holland and put themselves in this kind of boat with this kind of a crew and pay a big buck to tackle the North Atlantic. The North Atlantic is the graveyard of all kinds of ships including the Titanic and all kinds of fishing vessels.
I say that the Opposition is dead wrong. Nobody who cares about these people should attempt to send out a signal that they should leave that protection, get on a boat and put their life and health at risk to sail across the North Atlantic.
Yes, this country has a generosity of spirit for the true refugee who is fleeing oppression and needs our protection. However, it is wrong to signal to these people in trouble that they should put their health and safety in the hands of people like that.
Members will remember that two boatloads arrived on our East Coast. The ship's captain put them in lifeboats in the North Atlantic without adequate food, without adequate clothing, and without adequate shelter. That is how the Tamils got here.
A leaky tug with none of the things to protect health and safety brought the Sihks. The ship's captain brought that big ocean-going liner, not into a safe harbour with a wharf, but up to the shoreline in an area where people familiar with that part of the coastline would never have dared to attempt it. There were two boatloads. One was set adrift in the North Atlantic, and the second was put in a situation in which it could have capsized and all the people could have drowned so fast that it would have made your head spin.
This Chamber should send a signal to those desperate people in those conditions of safety not to put their lives in the hands of those kinds of people. That is the signal which this Party thinks is the best, most humane signal to send. That is why this Party and the members of it are so much in favour of this Bill.
