Hon. Warren Allmand (Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine
East): Mr. Speaker, once again we are faced with this Draconian Bill, Bill C-84, which reverses Canada's longstanding policy with respect to refugees. In order to block a small percentage of fraudulent refugees, the Government has introduced these measures which will also prevent legitimate refugees from getting into this country. This is a case of massive overkill with respect to the problem.
I have been listening in this debate to Members from the government side suggesting that the opposition to this Bill is simply being made by the members of the Liberal and New Democratic Parties. What nonsense. One need only look at the list of those who have time and again come out against this Bill. It includes nearly all the churches in Canada, the Canadian Civil Liberties Union, the Canadian Jewish Congress, B'Nai Brith Canada, associations of students, labour unions and all the groups that work with refugees and immigrants. Above all, the report of the Senate which is before us in the form of this amended Bill is supported by the Conservatives in the Senate.
The Senate report to amend this Bill is a unanimous report of Liberal and Conservative Senators. Therefore, the suggestion that the opposition to this Bill is simply an opposition by Liberal and New Democratic Party Members here in the House is nonsense. There is overwhelming opposition to this Bill not only throughout the country but even by those members of the Conservative Party in the Senate who signed the unanimous report with respect to this Bill and sent it back to the House. We were recalled to the House in the middle of the summer adjournment in 1987 to deal with what the Government described as an emergency. They brought us back

and asked us to deal with Bill C-84 immediately. Of course, the Bill required hearings and an extensive debate, not a filibuster. It demanded an extensive debate because the issues involved in the Bill were extremely serious.
After we entered the regular session in September, the Government had a higher priority for other matters and called in all sorts of other Bills. It did not consider this to be a high priority Bill, which did not justify the so-called emergency crisis for which we were brought back in the middle of August.
The Government has the right to call whatever Bill it wants every day. It simply did not call this Bill. Of course, it always wanted an agreement from the Opposition to dispose of it in one or two days. However, we would not agree to that because the issues are too important.
If the Government really pul a high priority on this Bill, since it has the right to fix the business of the House, it could have continued with the Bill until it was passed. Rather, it called the Bill now and then, here and there, and finally it was passed through the House. The Opposition tried to amend the Bill and voted against it, but the Government passed it as it wished, in its still imperfect form.
The Senate has not defeated the Bill but has returned it with certain very specific amendments. The Government accuses opposition Members of filibustering the Bill and delaying a solution to the issues. The Plaut commission was appointed by the former Liberal Government prior to the 1984 election. The Plaut commission reported in June, 1985, after the election, and made very specific recommendations about what should be done to renew our refugee legislation and avoid the problems being experienced due to the large numbers applying, fraudulent claims and so on. However, the Government did not respond to the Plaut report or bring in immediate legislation.
We then saw the two reports of November and December, 1985, from the parliamentary committee on immigration. They essentially agreed with the conclusions of the Plaut report and recommended certain legislation to correct the abuses and prevent fraudulent refugees from coming to this country. Once again, however, the Government did not act on those committee reports which were unanimous reports from members of the Liberal Party, Conservative Party and New Democratic Party.
The Government did not even introduce its own legislation at that time as a response to the reports. The Plaut commission and the Standing Committee on Labour, Employment and Immigration recommended a new, fast, efficient and fair system to deal with refugee claimants in order to weed out the fraudulent ones from legitimate ones, and discourage fraudulent claims in the future. Obviously, quick action on refugee claims, turning down those which are not legitimate, will discourage people from coming to this country to make such claims. Long delays of two or three years in making a decision encourage fraudulent claims, but the standing committee and Plaut report recommended solutions that were fast, efficient and fair. However, the Government did not act.
Immigration Act, 1976
The Plaut report was issued in June, 1985. It took the Government almost two years, until May, 1987, to table its legislation, Bill C-55. Now it is accusing the Opposition of delay and filibuster when it took it nearly two years to present a Bill on this important issue.
We believed that Bill C-55, although we identified flaws and imperfections in it, was the Government's solution to this question. However, just a few months later, in the middle of the summer, it presented Bill C-84, with further changes. This merely indicates the confusion of the Government. Perhaps it will introduce another Bill next week if there is another boat on our shore.
It does not really know what the solution is. It told us that Bill C-55 was the solution, then presented Bill C-84 a few months later. Now a committee report from the Senate, including Conservative Senators, states that while they believe the problem must be solved, and do not want to admit fraudulent refugees in this country, they suggest the Government is engaged in overkill and will only harm legitimate refugee claimants.
I must remind the House that a former Liberal Government signed the International Convention on Refugees in 1969. As a result of signing that treaty, we committed Canada to accepting refugees as defined by the treaty. We committed ourselves to that. We put it into legislation in 1976 as part of the law of the land. If someone was a legitimate refugee, as defined by the international convention, we had to accept them. These are people fleeing their country because their lives are in danger because of their politics, religion, race, language or whatever. They come to this country and we are obliged to receive them. However, we have a right to determine whether they are true refugees in accordance with the definition. The problem was that due to the conditions of the world, there were almost 20 million refugees fleeing horrible conditions in various countries, and the numbers increased. Canada had to change its procedures to deal with those claims quickly.
Rabbi Plaut, the parliamentary committee, the Liberal Party and, I believe, the New Democratic Party, all want to solve the problem. We want to solve the problem so that those who claim refugee status get a fair hearing. Those who are fraudulent, of course, we can send back, but they have a right to a hearing. The Supreme Court of Canada has already made a statement on that point when it said we must not only review the documentation but that they have a right to an oral hearing.
I believe that if this legislation passes as it is, and many experts have already said this, it will be overruled by the Supreme Court because it is contrary to our Constitution. Certain amendments have been proposed to Bill C-84 by the Senate. These are amendments dealing with serious matters such as the penalties to be imposed against those who help

January 29, 1988
Immigration Act, 1976
refugees, the turning back of boats, and so on. These amendments by the Senate were approved unanimously by the committee. Let us make that absolutely clear. What is interesting is that the Government accepted some of the amendments suggested by the Senate. They were minor, but they were accepted. This indicates that the Government recognized that there were flaws in its Bill. Otherwise it would not have accepted any amendments. It accepted minor amendments from the Senate to improve the Bill, but points dealing with human rights and liberties, with the human condition of individuals, it has not accepted, despite overwhelming support for those amendments by all sorts of groups in this country.
I want to point out again that the numbers of refugees coming to this country today are not out of line with those who came to this country in previous years. I would like to refer to those numbers because I think Canadians should be reminded. In 1982, we accepted 16,900 refugees from three special movements. That was in addition to the refugees we accepted under ordinary movements. There were 16,900 refugees in 1982, 9,300 from Poland, 3,000 plus from El Salvador, and 2,500 from Iran. In the period of 1978-79 we accepted over
11.000	refugees from Lebanon. This was a special movement over and above those who came in on regular movements. In the period of 1976-77, we accepted over 9,000 Vietnamese and Cambodians. In the period from 1975-78, we accepted over
7.000	Chileans and Argentinians. In the period 1972-73, we accepted 7,100 Ugandan Asians. In 1969 Canada accepted
12.000	Czechs following the aborted revolution in Czechoslovakia. In 1957, when our population was much smaller, we accepted 37,000 Hungarians, following the aborted revolution in that country. After the Second World War in 1945, Canada accepted 186,000 displaced persons. At that time our population was only 15 million. What has happened to all those people, the Hungarians, the Czechs, the Ugandans, the Chileans, the Vietnamese, the Lebanese, the Poles, the Salvadorans and the Iranians? They settled pretty well in this country. They have made a contribution. They started businesses and built homes. They are consumers. Very few of them are getting in trouble with the law, probably fewer than Canadians like myself.
We see these people out there in our multicultural environment. We know they are there and we do not regret the fact that we accepted these large waves of immigrants. But because there were two boatloads of refugees who came to our shores, a relatively small number, the Government panicked in response to some reactionary Canadians and brought in this legislation. This legislation is unwarranted. Everyone has been telling the Government that, but it is not listening. Why do we have this situation in the world? I mentioned that we have approximately 20 million refugees in the world. Again, I remind the House that since 1945, which was the end of the last war, there have been 150 regional wars. Those 150 regional wars have resulted in 20 million deaths. Two thirds of those deaths were civilian and 16 million of those 20 million deaths were in the Third World. In addition to the deaths resulting from those conflicts,
we also have a vast movement of refugees, particularly from Afghanistan, the Middle East, Indo-China, Iran, Sri Lanka, Central America and Latin America.
As I said earlier, Canada signed the international treaty with respect to refugees in 1969. We confirmed those obligations in 1976, putting them into law. We have committed ourselves to accepting legitimate refugees. We won the Nansen award a year and a half ago for our treatment of refugees, which is a tribute to Canadians in general. By adopting this legislation, we are throwing mud in the faces of those who presented us with that award.
I suggest to this House that if we are truly citizens of the world, we have a responsibility to help relocate and care for these refugees. As Canadians, we must ask ourselves if we are doing our fair share. The numbers we brought in in the past was not bad, but we have to ask ourselves continually, in the face of the tremendous crisis and tragedy we see in the world, are we as Canadians doing our fair share? Will be be doing our fair share by passing this Bill? Are we going to close our borders and shift the burden to someone else? Are we going to say: "Let the other guy do it. We have enough here by adopting the kind of measures in this Bill? No, we cannot shirk our responsibility. We cannot pass the buck. As I pointed out, since the Second World War, we have settled hundreds of thousands of refugees. We did it then and we can do it again.

What is it that prevents them from going back to their countries in many cases? It is the fact that there is economic manipulation and exploitation in El Salvador. I was very disappointed when the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) recently went to Central America. He ended up giving a very small amount of additional aid to Nicaragua, which all aid agencies say is a model in trying to deal with the problems of underdevelopment, but gave a much larger amount to Honduras, which is impeding the implementation of the Central American peace treaty and is serving as a base for the Contra revolutionaries to attack Nicaragua. In answer to the Hon. Member's question in a nutshell, the answer is for Canada to help with the underlying economic and social problems. We could do much more there. I have always felt that even under my own Government we were not doing enough. We have to do more if we want to change the conditions which lead to people fleeing their countries. If things were great in those countries, or at least improving, and if these people were being treated fairly and justly, then they would not want to be refugees. We should direct a great deal more of our attention there if we do not want all these people flooding our country, as the Conservatives do not seem to want. If they would pay more attention to solving the basic problems then they would not have boatloads of people on their doorstep.

Mr. Speaker, I must say that it is not with any great pleasure that I rise this afternoon once again to debate Bill C-84. It seems to me that it is deplorable that we have had to do this so many times with a repetition of many of the same points, and the same points that have been made by many responsible groups across Canada. Again today we are repeating ourselves.
Of course, we felt that it was a very impulsive response to incidents last summer which instigated this Bill to amend the Immigration Act in the first place. In my view, it was not necessary to take such a punitive and hysterical approach to a boatload of people who arrived on our eastern shores. It certainly was not necessary to respond in the manner in which the Government did. I remember last summer in Vancouver how Conservative Members, and I regret to say even the Hon. Member for Capilano (Mrs. Collins), was saying, "We have to get back to the House. This is a crisis". In turn, that type of response encouraged more and more people to become inflamed about a situation that it was not necessary to become so inflamed about.
1 know in my riding it resulted in many phone calls that had a racist tone. I very much regret that, instead of dealing with this in a positive manner, we were almost feeding into it by the way the Conservatives whipped us all back to Ottawa and said that we had to deal with this great crisis. That was on August 11, 1987. Here we are in late January, 1988, still dealing with this, and there does not seem to me to have been any great crisis at all.
The other thing I wish to say is that the Government has been stubborn and persistent in not making the changes that were obviously needed. The Government let the Bill go to the Senate, and now we have to go through this round again. Perhaps the Government did not want to listen to those of us in opposition. Perhaps the Government did not feel that we were being non-partisan in our comments. As Canadians, most of us do feel that the immigration and refugee policy is a humanitarian issue. It is not a partisan issue. We want to be sure it is just, and in the interest of both refugees and immigrants, as well as in the interests of Canada.
If the Government was not willing to listen to us, why did it not take very seriously the same type of comments that were coming from many independent groups across the country, people who had probably far more expertise than most of us in the House? In my riding there are refugee settlement groups, and groups of volunteers with a great deal of experience and commitment. Those groups have given much of their time without pay because they feel so strongly about this. They have spent a great deal of time helping to reach out and assist
Immigration Act, 1976
refugees or potential refugees and to provide support groups once they arrived in Canada.
Those groups certainly criticized this Bill in the same manner that we did, and in the same manner that the Senate has now done. Across the country there were immigration lawyers with great expertise who stated that many aspects of this Bill contravened the Charter of Rights. I understand from the analysis that the Senate has done that this is still the case. Yet, apparently the Government does not accept this.
Many church groups and humanitarian groups appealed on this matter. People, like Rabbi Plaut, who indeed has great expertise, have been trying for years to reform our immigration policy in order that we could handle it more effectively and not have the type of chaotic situation that we had last summer, and still have. There were many recommendations from Members of the House, and ones that were presented very seriously.
It was not always easy to take the opposition side last summer. This was an issue that people felt very strongly about. The Government's interpretation of the so-called crisis did not help people to look at it in a rational and objective manner.
Since last summer, I have met with a number of groups. The concern about this Bill and Bill C-55 has continued in many meetings that I have attended. In Vancouver East we have a great number of immigrants, people arriving from many different countries, for example, many countries in Asia, the South Pacific, and from Spanish-speaking countries in Central and South America.
Many groups have formed in support of immigrants and refugees. I recall a very large meeting that was held at the native education centre in Vancouver. It was very interesting to note that the native people were the ones who hosted this meeting, yet it was a meeting of people from a range of backgrounds who were very worried about Bill C-84 and Bill C-55. At that meeting there was a woman from the United States who was a refugee support person. She was helping refugees who wanted to come to Canada to get to the border. She was extremely concerned, especially with regard to Salvadorans and Guatemalans. She was quite convinced that they would be forcibly sent back to their countries and not allowed to come into Canada. She had no way of helping them once they got to that state either.
There was a very senior representative of the Anglican Church, I recall. I know the Hon. Member for Spadina (Mr. Heap) would know about this. This representative has been in the forefront of helping refugees not only in Canada but worldwide. Senior people of his church had been meeting and taking very strong positions. They were very concerned about these Bills. There were lawyers from Simon Fraser University who had a great deal of expertise. I was particularly impressed with native leaders who said, "This is unfair. We don't want people to be treated in this way". Most groups who were there

formed a coalition to oppose these Bills, and I hope they will continue to oppose them because both Bills are contrary to many things that most Canadians believe in.
Why do we oppose Bill C-84? Again, we have said this many times, but I want to repeat it. The New Democratic Party strongly opposed Bill C-84 in the Commons when it was here in the last round. It is monstrously unfair both to refugees and to Canadians who help refugees. It violates our Charter of the U.N. Convention on Refugees. I heard a Member from Vancouver Island a moment ago saying that the Bill does not contravene any of the U.N. conventions. This, however, does not seem to be the opinion of other experts. The Senate held hearings and heard some 37 witnesses after the Bill was passed in the House of Commons. There were lots of complaints about how much time the Senators were taking. It is unfortunate the Senate had to make all the amendments because the Bill should have been amended more strongly when it was here in the House. That is the House of Commons' job. It is our job as parliamentarians, elected to this House, to be responsive. It is the Government's job to be far more responsive and to integrate amendments that are valid and amendments that were proved to be matters that offended the Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
The Government accepted very few amendments. The Minister of Immigration (Mr. Bouchard), in particular was extremely obstinate and stubborn. I do not like to say that about anyone but I am afraid that this is the way he appeared to me. He was determined to push this Bill through, that he was right and the public of Canada was wrong.
As I said, the Bill went to the Senate. The Senate held hearings and heard 37 witnesses, many of whom appeared at the legislative committee in the Commons on Bill C-84. All of these witnesses, except immigration staff-and one knows to whom they are accountable-criticized the Bill and opposed it, all 37 of them. The Senate made 13 amendments before it adopted the Bill. As Members know, these have been set out in the Minutes of the Proceedings of the Senate for Tuesday, December 15. The 13 amendments remedy nearly all of the objections made by the witnesses. We commend the Senators for that job. We do not think it is their role. We think that job should have been done here in the House. All of those amendments were ones which the New Democratic Party had spoken to and had presented in the House.
These amendments remedy those parts of the Bill considered to offend the Charter of Rights and Freedoms. Surely that is a standard against which to measure policies that are implicit in this Bill. Why on earth is the Government so obstinate in not accepting amendments that are trying to make this Bill concur with the requirements of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms? As I understand it, if this Bill is tested again in the courts it will be back to square one and there will be a need for changes once more. The government knows what the criticisms are. Why would the Government not try to make the Bill conform completely to the Charter of Rights and Freedoms? That is why we have our Charter of Rights. If the Government rejects
all or most of these amendments in its coming motion to the Commons, we feel that we must oppose it.
May I quickly just review what the amendments are without going into any detail and as well review the Government's response? Amendment 1 clarifies the purposes of the Bill as opposing clandestine entry rather than smuggling. Then we have the whole question of security certificates in Amendments 2 and 3, which restore the right of a person accused of being a security risk to hear the case against him or her except where a judge decides that that would endanger national security or the safety of persons. Then there is the right of claim to refugee status covered by Amendment 4 from the Senate. This restores the right of a person accused of being a security risk nevertheless to have his refugee claim determined so that even people who may be a security risk have the right to due process. This would keep Canada's obligation under the U.N. convention relating to the status of refugees intact and enable the person, if deported, to have U.N. assistance in finding a safe country other than the one he or she has fled.
Another point is that of turning ships around. This seems to me to be the one most impractical and illogical. I was appalled when I heard the comment from the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Turner)-and again I was surprised he was so impulsive when he gave his reaction-that he agreed that ships coming to our East Coast should be sent back to sea without people having a just hearing. I notice that his critics thereafter took opposite points of view.

subtopic: IMMIGRATION ACT, 1976 MEASURE TO AMEND-CONSIDERATION OF SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity at this fairly late hour in our Friday session to speak on Bill C-84 and the Senate amendments. I guess I start off with a feeling of astonishment. After months of debate here and in committee where I was involved, we are still debating the issue and facing a filibuster. This is the end of the fourth day of debate on this issue this week and it is obvious that the opposition Parties are trying to draw out the debate.
I would like to ask them this question. Are they prepared to take the responsibility for the refugees who are not legitimate and who are continuing to come to our borders? Bill C-84 has not yet received Royal Assent, we do not have the legislative tools we need, so are they willing to take responsibility for those people?
I am sure they are aware of the really astonishing numbers. In 1980 only 1,600 people claimed refugee status. Obviously it was not a problem. However, because of world problems and changes which have taken place, we were faced with 30,000 people claiming refugee status in 1987. We know that on average 70 per cent of those people are not genuine refugees. Even of the remaining 30 per cent, about half already have protection in some other country. They are coming to Canada basically to improve their economic status. That is understandable, but that is not the purpose of the refugee system.
We have a backlog of thousands and thousands of people in the refugee system, 70 per cent of whom are not genuine refugees, and they should not be here. Under the rules we have set down, by all international criteria, those people should not be here. It is not fair to them or to genuine refugees who are being held up because of the backlog. It is more difficult for them to get on with their lives and the whole thing is blatantly unfair.
I found it interesting that my friend from Vancouver East accused me in her remarks of inflaming the situation. Last

August, when we had a boatload of people coming to our shores off Halifax, I, like many of my colleagues, as well as my constituents, concerned about maintaining the integrity of the refugee system, called for the recall of Parliament and tough new legislation to remedy the situation. That was not inflaming the situation. That was a legitimate concern expressed by millions of Canadians across this country and Members in this House who wanted something done about the situation.
1 am appalled that for month after month we have been faced with this obstructionism. Even this week, as hundreds of people come to our borders, this situation is creating false expectations. It is cruel. It is inhumane. Members of the NDP may claim they are the Party of humanity and genuine compassion, but I do not agree. This is unfair and I ask them, as I did last summer and last fall when we debated this Bill, let us get on with it, get the rules in place so people around the world will know what they are and will not come here under false pretenses.
We are sometimes accused, because of Bill C-84 and its companion, Bill C-55, which is still in the Senate, of lacking compassion. That is not true. Neither are Canadians lacking in compassion. The record shows very clearly the exact opposite.
We are a country of immigrants. My father emigrated from England around 1917. I am sure the parents of most of the people in this House, in fact many Members themselves, have come here as immigrants. We have a long-standing reputation for tolerance and compassion. I think that is so important. I care about it so much that I do not want to see it undermined because people are getting frustrated by what they feel is abuse of that genuine sense of tolerance and compassion. Unfortunately, that is what 1 have seen happen over the past months. People feel that Parliament is not dealing quickly enough with this issue.
We have a comprehensive system of aid for refugees. I have dealt with refugee organizations in Vancouver, Mosaic and others, who do excellent work. We as a Government have continued with the funding required to assist those groups. We received the Nansen Medal in 1986 for our response to refugees. The measures we have in Bill C-84, to my mind, do not negate that tradition. They deal with a new reality which requires different measures than were required in the past. What we want to do is to respond to genuine refugees. Over the years we have been very effective, but in recent years that effectiveness has been reduced because of the acceleration in the number of people who arrive here claiming refugee status when they are not refugees.
We all know there are people who try to use the refugee system to profit from those who want to come to Canada. We heard the stories last summer. We saw examples even last fall. It was evident that these people had been counselled to come to Canada, after paying money to someone in their own country, and claim refugee status. It was very evident that they were not genuine refugees. They were economic migrants looking for a better life. That is fine, but it is not fair that they should
Immigration Act, 1976
jump the queue. There are of course many people who would like to come to Canada in the regular immigration stream, but we have rules, regulations and quotas and people have to follow the rules or else you get these outbursts of frustration and antagonism which I have seen in many parts of the country about our over-all immigration system. I do not think it is fair, but because people feel the refugee situation has gotten out of control they damn the total immigration system.
Obviously we have to deal with these unscrupulous swindlers. We have to have measures in place which will ensure that they do not get off scot-free as has happened in the past. Bill C-84 will put many of those measures in place. Those kinds of people abuse our system for their own benefit. That in itself has reduced our ability to deal with genuine refugees. Because of the massive numbers already backlogged in the system, frustration has been caused to those who want the system to help the genuine refugee. That is what this Bill is directed toward.
There are thousands of people experiencing life-threatening dangers who came to Canada as refugees. They include people displaced by World War II and the refugees from Uganda who arrived in the early 1970s, many of whom are on the West Coast and have been wonderful citizens. They include more than 100,000 Indo-Chinese refugees who arrived here between 1970 and 1985 and thousands of refugees from Central and South America brought to Canada under special measures. Canadians welcome these unfortunate people with open arms. On behalf of Canadians we now seek to protect the meaning of "refugee status" because it seems to have taken on a new meaning and has caused confusion.
As I mentioned, in 1987 almost 30,000 people arrived in this country claiming refugee status. The dramatic jump which took place between 1985 and 1987 means that there are 44,000 people at one stage or another of the process. Because of the Charter of Rights and an appropriate desire for the rule of law, it is a long system with appropriate checks and balances.
In Bill C-55 we have introduced some changes to tighten up and streamline that system so that decisions can be made more quickly. We know that among those 44,000 there is a large number of economic migrants. It is pretty hard for them to get on with their lives if they are here under the pretense of being genuine refugees but are really economic migrants. If they are deported at the end of the process, they could have wasted anywhere from two to five years of their lives. That is not fair to them.
We have heard stories of this and the Government looks awful because it deported them, but they did not follow the rules, they were not genuine refugees, and I think the expectation of citizens of this country is that under those circumstances they should not stay. Therefore, they must once once again go through the process of displacement. That is an

January 29, 1988
Immigration Act, 1976
extremely unfortunate outcome of a situation in which we are not able to pass laws and deal with situations appropriately.
In the past year and a half we were confronted with two very highly publicized incidents of irregular arrivals on our shores. It was these two incidents which caused the outburst and reaction. 1 am not sure that most Canadians realize that approximately 500 people per week come to Canada claiming refugee status. Because of the media attention which surrounded those two incidents they brought the issue to the fore of people's minds and demanded a response from the Government.
1 do not want myself or my colleagues to be misunderstood on this issue. Canadians want to help genuine refugees. Through government sponsorship and dedication and thousands of private sponsors, church groups, and other organizations, we maintain a compassionate tradition. Millions of dollars are spent helping refugees adjust and settle when they arrive in Canada. We also show our commitment through international organizations to assist refugees. Food aid is a major component of economic assistance and service to refugees, both through the Government and the voluntary sector. There have been many programs during the past three years which are very important in that regard.
We understand the anger of Canadians over the blatant abuse of our refugee system. As borders around the world shut down Canada becomes more vulnerable to such abuse. Bill C-84 protects genuine refugees and legitimate immigrants. This legislation is carefully aimed at a very small minority, the smugglers who bring people in illegally and the conspirators who take advantage of the generosity of Canadians and the desperation and gullibility of would-be migrants. Canadians have been angered by this abuse of our system and horrified by the traffic in human misery which it generates.
We do not want to deny protection to those in genuine need. It is time to redefine just whom we want to help, to make it clear that our refugee policy exists to aid refugees, and that within this policy the person who claims refugee status must merit it. As well, we must make it clear that people who flaunt Canada's immigration laws will not get away with it. They must be shown that they can no longer be allowed to make a mockery of our country and our genuine generosity.
As they say, there is no one more angry than a person wronged. We have been very genuine in our generosity and when our generosity is abused it does cause a backlash. People really went out of their way and are now being taken advantage of. We must ensure that that does not exist in our country.
I hope that my colleagues in both opposition Parties see the importance of this Bill and move quickly to give it final approval. The Senate has recommended various amendments. We have accepted some of the amendments, either in whole or in principle, but 11 of them we cannot accept. The Minister has gone through them one by one as could I. I have looked at them carefully and was involved in discussing them in
committee. They just would not make sense. They would undermine the Bill and would not allow it to accomplish what 1 believe it should accomplish.
For example, Canadians do not want people who have committed a serious crime in another country to have the right to make a refugee claim. That is the kind of thing about which they are angry.
We must be able to turn ships away. The Minister has agreed to an amendment which would provide for this only in exigent circumstances. The responsible Minister will have to be involved in such a decision, so safeguards are included. However, we have ensured that this will be in compliance with our obligations under the convention and will take into account the safety and health of the passengers.
This would obviously be an extraordinary measure. However, in those extraordinary circumstances where the information is clear that a boatload of persons will be arriving on our shore and the evidence is that they are not genuine refugees, the Minister must have those powers. It is obviously a deterrent power which we hope we will not have to use. We hope that it will send a signal to the international community and that it and the accompanying increased fines will stop such carriage of people around the world.
The Senate made other suggestions on limiting search and seizure to daytime hours. That is unrealistic in Canada. In the North there are no daytime hours in the winter-time. We would be totally stymied in dealing with a plane coming into the Arctic. We would not be able to use search and seizure methods for almost six months of the year. People would only make entry at night-time. It just does not make any sense if we seriously want to deal with the problem with which we are dealing in Bill C-84.
Those amendments put forward by the Senate are not acceptable. They would seriously undermine the objectives of this Bill. I believe that the most important thing which we must accomplish through this Bill and the accompanying Bill, C-55, is to reassure the Canadian public that this Parliament, including all Members on all sides, have a genuine concern about maintaining the basic integrity of our refugee system, with the provisions of this Bill we will indeed have in place the necessary safeguards to ensure that that occurs.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Capilano (Mrs. Collins) urged haste in passing this legislation. Let me remind her that the Plaut report was tabled in 1985. Instead of acting on it, the Government referred it to the Standing Committee on Labour, Employment and Immigration. When it finally acted, it was not in the humane and reasoned manner as prescribed by Rabbi Plaut who said that declaring a claimant to be a refugee is not a privilege we grant but a right we recognize. Instead, the Government took some very negative measures that will cause much difficulty for legitimate refugees.
I would like the Member to deal particularly with the section dealing with aiding and abetting. It does not distinguish between people who are working with refugees, many of whom do not have proper documentation since that is part of the fact of being a refugee, and those unscrupulous immigration agents who use the refugee process as a way of getting people here. The Government is using a scatter-gun approach, and many people in church groups and refugee aid groups are very concerned, with good reason, that this legislation can be used to target them for their activities which the majority of Canadians believe are perfectly legitimate.
The Government says that it has no intention of targeting those people, but has not brought in the kind of amendments that would exempt them. Surely if the Government is in the process of writing legislation it should be able to do so in a way that will target more specifically the kinds of people at whom it is aiming, and not take the scatter-gun approach that will harm innocent citizens who are working to help genuine refugees in Canada?

Mr. Speaker, I thank the Hon. Member for Capilano (Mrs. Collins) for her response to the Member for Cowichan-Malahat-The Islands (Mr. Manly) in the matter of the Attorney General's permission. However, I would ask her to consider whether it is not an unsatisfactory and even an unfair writing of the law to write the law so that it describes the actions of thousands of Canadians, including for example, a person who recently won the Pearson Medal for Peace, Nancy Pocock, for a good many kinds of peace activity but in the last half dozen years primarily doing the very thing that is described in the Act, namely assisting undocumented persons to come to Canada.

I am not talking about whether she is a Member of Parliament, whether she is a member of a church, whether she is ordained, whether she is a nun. It is not a question of who it is, it is a question of what the person is doing. Is it in accordance with the law or not in accordance with the law?
As the law is written, there is no distinction between what she does when she goes, say, to Fort Erie and conducts a Salvadoran refugee claimant across the bridge and, at the first step into Canada, takes him to the immigration office and says, "This Salvadoran without a visa is claiming refugee status in Canada. He has grounds to say he cannot return to Salvador and it will not be safe for him to return even to the United States". Of course, that becomes the matter of the Immigration Department, to put the process in motion to determine whether his claim is justifiable.
But that has been regarded entirely as a legal action up until Bill C-84 was introduced. People have been praised for that and praised for it by the Minister, by Members of the Government and, as I say, by orders of the Peace Medal and the Governor General who presented it.
Surely it is unsatisfactory to say that that is illegal, but to suggest that on a sort of person by person basis, if the Attorney General or his deputy likes the colour of her eyes he will say: "We won't prosecute you", surely it is necessary in law to say what it is that we are objecting to, and surely what we are objecting to is the attempt to deceive or to cheat, that is to get a person in, as one Hon. Member said a few moments ago, by circumventing the law. That suggests hiding, sneaking, smuggling, coming in secretly or dishonestly with lies or by evading the proper officials.
Surely it is necessary to distinguish between the person who evades or seeks to evade and a person who seeks not to evade but to go directly to the appropriate legal authorities. Will the Hon. Member not accept that a law is much more workable when it does not require the Attorney General to exempt the majority of Canadians who are condemned under that law?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to participate in this debate once again today. One would have wished that the Government would have seen the light after all the controversy it has caused with this Bill and would have decided at least to heed the recommendations of the Senate and the recommendations that opposition Members have suggested in a very positive way.
Let us remember where we come from when we are discussing this Bill. First, we know that in 1983 or 1984 it became apparent that the number of applicants to become refugees was increasing at a substantial rate. The Government appointed a commission under Rabbi Gunther Plaut and the commission produced a report in 1985 which made certain recommendations to the Government. Meanwhile, the flow of refugee claimants coming to this country was increasing at an
accelerated rate. The intensity was increasing dramatically as time went by.	'
In 1986 there was again a marked increase in the numbers of refugee applicants, to the point where last summer we had somewhere in the order of 18,000 people claiming refugee status in the space of a year. One day last summer, Canadians discovered that 174 people had landed on the coast of the Maritimes. What was the first reaction of Canadians when that happened? It was the usual reaction we expect, the reaction of tolerance and kindness which we have displayed historically to newcomers to this land. The first gesture, I believe, by Canadians at that time was to offer sandwiches and tea to these new people. I was proud that first day. However, that pride was very short-lived.
I saw not long afterwards messages coming from the Government side which seemed to feed on that unfortunate small element of intolerance that is ever so present in any society. With the encouragement, in my view, of the Government, people began to resent the arrival of these people. The whole incident was not even taken into context. I said moments ago that 18,000 people had made application in one year and that on one day 174 of them arrived. We must realize that not a week goes by in which we do not have 174 applicants. But this incident created national attention because they arrived all at once in a manner I described initially, and then in another manner which was not as pleasant, at least not pleasant for me as a Canadian to see.
The Government then took its next step. It decided this country was being invaded by refugees. It asked the Speaker to reconvene Parliament to deal with this so-called crisis. Initially, of course, the Speaker was reluctant to accept this proposition but, of course, it is not the Speaker's role to govern and for that I do not criticize the Chair. It is the Government's role to govern. The Government called back the House and brought forward Bill C-84, which has everything to do with satisfying the right-wing element and very little to do with assisting the refugee process, tightening it up or making it better for our country.
What this country really needed was to have a new refugee policy some three years ago at the time when both opposition Parties asked for it. But the Government did not produce it. It initially had the report and it did not do anything with it. It referred the matter to a parliamentary committee. The parliamentary committee made a report and the Government did not do anything with that. The Government acted swiftly when the issue became something we saw on national television that day last summer.

What the Government, what the party in power today should have done three years ago is take steps to ensure that competent staff was in place when people arrived in Canada and applied for refugee status. Instead of waiting two years to determine a person's refugee status, we should have a policy aimed at determining that status within four to six weeks. If

that were the case, Mr. Speaker, a person who applies for refugee status and is sent back to his country four to six weeks later will not be as likely to come right back if that person was making a false claim. On the other hand, people with valid claims would always have the assurance of being allowed to settle in this country, and I think that is what we all want. We want to separate those who make phony claims from those whose claims are genuine. Unfortunately, the present Bill is not satisfactory in this respect.
